guide.title: Big Moose Mountain, Maine: a divided mountain above Moosehead Lake
guide.intro: Big Moose Mountain, long marketed as Squaw Mountain or Big Squaw, is today operated by Friends of the Mountain, a group the operator's own website describes as "A non-profit 501c(3) community ski area since 2012." The mountain is split in two. Per the operator's own site, "We offer lift service on a triple chair to the lower mountain and a beginner conveyor lift for our newest skiers." The upper mountain has had no lift since March 7, 2004, when, according to New England Ski History's Big Moose Mountain page, "a chair grip on the upper mountain double chairlift failed, resulting in four injuries. As a result, lift served skiing on the upper mountain ceased." The operator's own pricing page now sells an "Upper Mountain VIP Card" including "one (1) passenger cat ride to the summit of Big Moose Mountain, full uphill access," for named backcountry trails that "are not accessible by chairlift service."

sections.heading: From idle years to a $1-a-year lease
sections.body: According to New England Ski History, owner James Confalone offered Piscataquis County a $1 per year, 30-year lease on the ski area in August 2010; the county declined, and the area did not operate in 2010-11 or 2011-12. Starting in 2012, per the same source, "a group named The Friends of Squaw Mountain procured a $1 per year lease from Confalone and worked to reopen the ski area with many donations and volunteer labor." After sitting idle for two seasons, the mountain "reopened with its triple chairlift on February 10, 2013," logging 70 days of operation the following season.

sections.heading: The upper mountain, by snowcat
sections.body: In October 2023, NewEnglandSkiIndustry.com reported that Friends of the Mountain had entered into an agreement to acquire a 13-passenger snowcat from Parshall, Colorado, noting the upper mountain had been without chairlift service since the 2004 accident; a Borvig triple chairlift served the lower mountain terrain as of that date, per the same report. In December 2024, per NewEnglandSkiIndustry.com, Friends of the Mountain announced a partnership with the Moosehead Lake Region Economic Development Corporation, aiming "to raise $5.95 million to acquire 1,716 acres featuring the ski area, building on the $1.2 million previously raised for reopening and improvements." The campaign's leader, Amy Lane, was quoted saying, "Only by placing this mountain in nonprofit hands will we be able to attract funding and build a financially sustainable ski destination for generations to come." The same report states a separate, unrelated $75 million resort redevelopment proposal was cancelled in November 2022, distinct from Friends of the Mountain's operation of the existing lift.

sections.heading: Passes and the campaign, today
sections.body: As of this writing, per the operator's own homepage, the fundraising banner reads "$2.6 Million Raised" against the "Save the View, Save the Mountain" campaign's $5.95 million goal, and the site separately thanks supporters for helping "make our 14th season such a success." The operator's own ticket-and-pricing page states 2026-2027 season passes are "Now on Sale," with published prices including an Adult pass at $450 and a 1st Grade-College pass at $400. Per the operator's own homepage, its address is 447 Ski Resort Road, Greenville Junction, ME 04442, an unincorporated village within the Town of Greenville.

sections.heading: In Greenville
sections.body: The Moosehead Marine Museum's own history page states, "In 1977, they founded the nonprofit Moosehead Marine Museum, acquiring the Katahdin as its star exhibit," adding that "in 1979 the 'Kate' was added to the National Register of Historic Places." Indian Hill Trading Post's own website lists Irving fuel available "24/7" alongside a Shop 'N Save supermarket, outdoor apparel and gear, and Maine-made products. Stress Free Moose Pub's own website describes it as offering "Drinks, live music, pub grub, and a mellow atmosphere on the shores of Moosehead Lake in Greenville, Maine."

faq.question: Why is Big Moose Mountain split into a lower and an upper mountain?
faq.answer: A chairlift accident on March 7, 2004 ended lift service to the upper mountain, per New England Ski History. The lower mountain still runs a triple chair and a beginner conveyor, per the operator's own site, while the upper mountain's trails are reachable only by a paid snowcat ride or by uphill travel.

faq.question: Who operates Big Moose Mountain today?
faq.answer: Friends of the Mountain, a non-profit that has run the lower mountain's lift since 2012-13, per New England Ski History, and that is separately raising funds to purchase the mountain outright, per NewEnglandSkiIndustry.com's 2024 reporting.

places.name: Moosehead Marine Museum
places.summary: A Greenville museum built around the historic steamship Katahdin, added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
places.history: The museum's own history page states, "In 1977, they founded the nonprofit Moosehead Marine Museum, acquiring the Katahdin as its star exhibit," and "In 1979 the 'Kate' was added to the National Register of Historic Places." Per the museum's own "Museum" page, it "houses a wide array of nautical treasures" and operates seasonally, with 2026 hours running June 16 through October 11, Tuesday through Saturday.

places.name: Indian Hill Trading Post
places.summary: A Greenville general store and gas stop serving the Moosehead Lake region.
places.history: Per the store's own website, it states, "No matter if you are planning a small family getaway, fanciful escape up north to the Moosehead Lake Region, or longer outdoors trip – we have nearly everything for any occasion," listing Irving fuel available "24/7" alongside a Shop 'N Save supermarket, outdoor apparel and gear, and Maine-made products.

places.name: Stress Free Moose Pub
places.summary: A Greenville pub on the shores of Moosehead Lake, serving lunch and dinner with live music.
places.history: Per the pub's own website, it describes itself as offering "Drinks, live music, pub grub, and a mellow atmosphere on the shores of Moosehead Lake in Greenville, Maine," with a "full menu for lunch and dinner, including pub grub & diner classics, soup, sandwiches, steaks, seafood & more."
